name: East Slope

waypoints.name: Thunder Creek Trailhead, Colonial Creek Campground
waypoints.note: Trail starts at the amphitheater in the campground's south loop off SR 20 (MP 130); NPS backcountry permit required for the overnight bivy.
waypoints.directions: The trailhead is at Colonial Creek Campground on SR 20, just past milepost 130 — turn into the campground and find the trail starting at the amphitheater in the south loop, at about 1,200 feet. A North Cascades National Park backcountry permit, available from the Marblemount Wilderness Information Center, is required for the overnight bivy at the Borealis Glacier.

waypoints.name: McAllister Camp
waypoints.note: Established NPS camp where McAllister Creek meets Thunder Creek; last easy, reliable water before leaving the valley floor.
waypoints.directions: Follow the Thunder Creek Trail south up the valley, roughly 6 to 6.7 easy miles for only about 700 ft of gain. The trail bridge over Thunder Creek near the camp has been reported out in past years, leaving a log crossing or a wade, so check current park trail conditions before you go.

waypoints.name: Tricouni Camp / leave-trail point for Lucky Ridge
waypoints.note: Camp sits in open salal forest just past a bridge over Fisher Creek; this is where climbers leave the maintained trail to gain Lucky Ridge toward Primus.
waypoints.directions: Continue south on the Thunder Creek Trail about 1.5 miles, crossing the bridge over Fisher Creek, to Tricouni Camp in open salal forest just beyond it, around 8 miles from the trailhead. This is where the climbers' path to Lucky Ridge leaves the maintained trail.

waypoints.name: Bivy at toe of Borealis Glacier
waypoints.note: Gravel bivy spots on the old streambed near the proglacial lake at the glacier's terminus, with a direct view of the icefall above; reached by climbing SSE up Lucky Ridge from Tricouni Camp.
waypoints.directions: Leave the valley trail on a short steep drop toward Thunder Creek and cross the creek before picking up the climbers' path on the far side; the first quarter to half mile is a bushwhack through devil's club and blowdown before the boot track becomes usable. It then climbs the ridge dividing McAllister and Thunder creeks, gaining roughly 4,000 ft in about two miles of steep forest, slide alder and finally larch and heather, to treeline and the gravel flats beside the lake at the glacier's toe.

waypoints.name: Borealis Glacier icefall
waypoints.note: Rope up at the bivy and stay on the glacier's eastern margin here — the lower and upper tiers are split by an icefall and cliff bands that have caught parties climbing too far climber's-left.
waypoints.directions: Rope up before stepping onto the ice. The glacier has retreated into a lower and an upper tier separated by an icefall and cliff bands, and picking the line that links them is the crux of the day; parties that commit to the wrong side get cliffed out above the lower tier. Scout it from the bivy in good light rather than working it out on the move.

waypoints.name: Lucky Pass (Primus-Tricouni col)
waypoints.note: Gain the col via the glacier's east margin; the East Ridge to Primus's summit starts here, with the Tricouni Peak route splitting off to the east.
waypoints.directions: Continue up the upper tier to the broad snow col between Primus and Tricouni at about 7,200 ft, weaving around crevasses. Moats open where the snow pulls back from rock later in the season, so test the edges before stepping across.

waypoints.name: Primus Peak
waypoints.note: True summit reached via 3rd-class scrambling along the East Ridge from Lucky Pass; descent reverses the same ridge and glacier line.
waypoints.directions: From the col turn up the ridge toward Primus, about 1,300 ft of Class 2-3 talus, scree and snow with no defined path. Where it steepens below a false summit around 8,270 ft, traverse climber's left around it rather than taking the steep snow head-on, then finish on easy blocks and a short run of kicked steps. The rock is loose enough that helmets matter more here than the grade implies.

approach: Start at the Thunder Creek Trailhead at Colonial Creek Campground on SR 20 (turn in just past milepost 130). Follow the Thunder Creek Trail roughly 6-6.7 miles to McAllister Camp, then continue past Tricouni Camp (~8 mi) and leave the maintained trail to climb the climbers' path up 'Lucky Ridge' to a bivy near the northeast corner of the lake at the toe of the Borealis Glacier (~6,000 ft). One detailed trip log (Aug. 2018) recorded 8.25 miles and 4,760 ft of gain from trailhead to this camp in about 9 hours. Note: the trail bridge over Thunder Creek near McAllister Camp has been reported washed out in past years, requiring a log crossing or wade — check current NPS trail-conditions postings before you go.

approach_variants.name: Thunder Creek and Lucky Ridge to the Borealis Glacier and Lucky Pass
approach_variants.notes:
Start at the Thunder Creek trailhead at Colonial Creek Campground on SR-20, just past milepost 130, near 1,200 ft. Follow the Thunder Creek Trail roughly six miles to McAllister Camp, then continue past Tricouni Camp around mile eight.

A ford of Thunder Creek at a log jam is normally required and the bridge near McAllister Camp has been out in past years — check current NPS conditions rather than assuming a dry crossing.

Leave the maintained trail at Tricouni Camp and climb the climbers' path up Lucky Ridge, the ridge between McAllister and Thunder creeks: roughly 4,000 ft of gain over a couple of miles through brush and devil's club, with two short cliff-band scrambles. Camp near the northeast corner of the proglacial lake at the toe of the Borealis Glacier around 6,000 ft, with the icefall in view above.

Rope up around 7,000 ft on the flat snow shelf and climb the glacier's eastern margin — the central icefall splits the lower and upper tiers and has caught parties who drifted climber's-left.
approach_variants.season: Mid-July through August, while enough of the Borealis Glacier's snowpack remains to bridge crevasses; by late September the glacier is largely bare and the pass can be bullet ice and loose rock
hazards: A mandatory Thunder Creek ford with a powerful current, worse later in the day as snowmelt rises
The central icefall on the Borealis Glacier — stay on the eastern margin
Hidden crevasses that open both vertically and horizontally, and moats where snow pulls off rock, worst late season
Cloud and fog that move in on this glacier routinely
A long, remote approach with no cell coverage
approach_variants.baseFinding:
The base is Lucky Pass at about 7,200 ft, and the pass identifies itself by what it divides: it is the notch at the head of the Borealis Glacier between Primus and Tricouni Peak, and the route to Tricouni splits off east from the same spot. If the ground only falls away on one side of you, you are not at the pass.

From the pass the east slope rises directly west — a bouldery class 3 slope, not a ridge crest and not a face. Parties describe the climbing above the pass as nothing more than a walk, which is the honest summary: the difficulty of this route is the creek, the brushy ridge and the glacier, all of which are behind you by the time you are at the pass.

The counting test is the false summit, and it is the one thing above the pass that can go wrong. A false summit stands at about 8,270 ft. You traverse climber's-left around it — you do not go over it — and the true summit at 8,508 ft is beyond. If you reached a high point without having traversed around anything, you are 240 ft short.

Negative test against the peak's other routes, and it works before you ever leave the car: this route is the only one reached from the Thunder Creek side. The South Ridge is reached from the Eldorado ice cap across five glaciers, and the North Ridge from an unnamed glacier north of the peak. If you walked up a creek trail from a campground on Highway 20, you are on this one.
